abstract: ABSTRACT Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is a common and debilitating complication of diabetes, in which oxidative stress and metabolic memory drive progressive nerve damage. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as important regulators in diabetic complications, but their roles in DPN remain poorly understood. RNA sequencing (RNA‐Seq) and Weighted Gene Co‐Expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) were performed to identify DPN‐associated circRNAs in rat sciatic nerves. Multi‐omics approaches, including proteomics and metabolomics, were applied to characterize the downstream pathways of circ_0000756. Functional studies in Schwann cells assessed oxidative stress, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses, while a DPN rat model was used to validate in vivo effects. Circ_0000756 was significantly upregulated in DPN, acting as an miR‐7b decoy to inhibit NRF2/ARE pathway activation. This led to enhanced oxidative stress, Schwann cell damage, and amplification of metabolic memory effects. Knockdown of circ_0000756 reduced oxidative stress and apoptosis in Schwann cells and mitigated nerve damage in DPN models. Circ_0000756 drives DPN progression by disrupting the miR‐7b/NRF2/ARE axis, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target for this challenging diabetic complication.

2.1
circRNA
‐Seq Analysis
Sciatic nerve tissues from 10 control and 10 DPN rats were used for total RNA extraction with TRIzol reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Genomic DNA was removed using DNase I (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and linear RNAs were digested with RNase R (Epicentre, USA) to enrich circRNAs. RNA quantity was measured with a NanoDrop 1000 spectrophotometer (NanoDrop Technologies, USA). For each sample, 3 μg of RNA was treated with the RiboMinus Eukaryote Kit (Qiagen, USA) to remove ribosomal RNA (rRNA). cDNA libraries were constructed following the Illumina TruSeq protocol and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform. Reads were aligned to the
Rattus norvegicus
reference genome (UCSC Genome Database) (
http://genome.ucsc.edu/
) using TopHat2, and circRNAs were identified with CIRI2. CircRNA abundance was quantified by back‐spliced junction reads. Differential expression was assessed with the edgeR package (v4.0.16), using |log2FoldChange| > 1 and
p
< 0.05 as significance thresholds.
2.2
WGCNA
WGCNA is an unsupervised method for constructing co‐expression networks from large‐scale transcriptomic data based on similarity in expression patterns, and for clustering genes (or circRNAs) into modules without prior assumptions. This approach is particularly useful for identifying potential molecular interaction networks. The “WGCNA” R package (v1.72‐5) was applied to construct co‐expression networks and detect DPN‐associated modules. Genes with high variance were first selected, and sample clustering was performed with the hclust function. A correlation matrix was generated using the Pearson algorithm, and the optimal soft‐thresholding power was chosen to convert it into a weighted adjacency matrix. The adjacency matrix was then transformed into a topological overlap matrix (TOM). Modules were identified by hierarchical clustering with the DynamicTreeCut algorithm, using a minimum size of 100 and a height cutoff of 0.25. Modules significantly correlated with DPN were considered clinically relevant.
2.3
Proteomics Analysis
Total protein was extracted from primary rat Schwann cells transfected with either short hairpin RNA‐circ_0000756 (sh‐circ_0000756) or short hairpin RNA‐negative control (sh‐NC) (
n
= 3 per group) using a protein lysis buffer containing 4% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 100 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.6). Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) analysis was performed using an Agilent nano‐LC system coupled with a QSTAR XL Q‐TOF mass spectrometer (Applied Biosystems). Data acquisition was conducted using a nano‐electrospray ionization (nano‐ESI) source and Analyst 1.1 software. Peptides were vacuum‐dried, dissolved in solution A, and loaded at 10 μL/min onto an SCX column (Bio‐SCX) and a C18 precolumn (PepMap). Fractionation was achieved by a 16‐step NaCl gradient, followed by separation on a VYDAC 218MS nanoflow reverse‐phase column using a 120‐min gradient. Mass spectra were acquired in positive ion mode with a spray voltage of 2.0 kV in information‐dependent acquisition (IDA) mode. Each 0.7‐s MS scan (400–1600 m/z) was followed by three 2‐s MS/MS scans (100–2000 m/z). Precursor ions > 25 counts/s were subjected to collision‐induced dissociation (CID). Peptides were identified using ProteinPilot 3.0 software (Applied Biosystems) with the Paragon algorithm against the rat protein database. A ProtScore > 1.3 and false discovery rate (FDR) < 1% were applied. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined using the edgeR R package (v4.0.16), with |log2FoldChange| > 1 and
p
< 0.05 as thresholds.

Primary Schwann Cell Isolation, Culture, and In Vitro Metabolic Memory Model Construction
Primary Schwann cells were isolated from sciatic nerves of neonatal male rats (≤ 4 days old, strain No. 101, Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd.). Lentiviral Infection and Experimental Grouping
Two short hairpin RNA (shRNA) sequences targeting KPNA4 were designed based on GenBank, with a non‐targeting shRNA (sh‐NC, SHC002, Sigma‐Aldrich) as control. Oligonucleotides were synthesized by GenePharma (Shanghai, China). Lentiviral vectors were constructed using the pLKO.1 backbone, and HEK293T cells at 80%–90% confluence were co‐transfected with packaging plasmids and target vectors using Lipofectamine 2000 (11668500, Thermo Fisher, USA). Dual‐Luciferase Reporter Assay
Luciferase reporter constructs containing either wild‐type (WT) or mutant (MUT) miR‐7b binding sites within circ_0000756 were synthesized (GenePharma, China) and cloned into the pmirGLO vector (Promega, USA), generating WT‐circ_0000756 and MUT‐circ_0000756. Similarly, WT and MUT constructs of the Keap1 3′UTR were prepared (WT‐Keap1 and MUT‐Keap1). Plasmids were co‐transfected with miR‐7b mimics or negative controls (miR‐NC) into 293 T cells (ATCC, USA) using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen, USA). After 48 h, luciferase activity was measured with the Dual‐Luciferase Reporter Assay System (Promega, USA), and firefly activity was normalized to Renilla activity to evaluate binding efficiency.

A biotin‐labeled circ_0000756 probe (Sangon, China) was incubated with cell lysates, and RNA–protein complexes were captured using streptavidin magnetic beads (88817, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). After washing, RNA was extracted, and the enrichment of miR‐7b was determined by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT‐qPCR). An unlabeled probe served as a negative control.

Cell lysates prepared with RIP lysis buffer containing protease and RNase inhibitors were incubated overnight at 4°C with anti‐Argonaute2 (Ago2, ab186733, Abcam, UK) or control IgG (ab172730, Abcam, UK). RNA co‐precipitated with proteins was eluted with RIP buffer containing proteinase K and analyzed by RT‐qPCR to assess Keap1 mRNA and miR‐7b enrichment.

To evaluate NRF2 protein stability, cells were treated with CHX (5 μM, 01810, Sigma‐Aldrich) and MG132 (20 μM, M7449‐1ML, Sigma‐Aldrich). Dimethyl Sulfoxide (DMSO) served as the vehicle control. Cells were harvested at 0, 2, 4, and 6 h, and NRF2 levels were analyzed by Western blot.

MG132
Treatment and Immunoprecipitation for Ubiquitination Detection
To assess NRF2 ubiquitination, cells were treated with 1 μM MG132 (M8699, Sigma‐Aldrich, USA) for 4 h to inhibit proteasome‐mediated degradation. Total protein (100 μg) was extracted and subjected to immunoprecipitation using Protein A Sepharose 4B fast‐flow beads (P9424‐5ML, Sigma‐Aldrich, USA). The NRF2 antibody (#12721, Cell Signaling Technology, USA) was crosslinked to Protein A Sepharose 4B beads, which were incubated with cell lysates overnight at 4°C with rotation. Beads were washed three times with lysis buffer (4°C, 5000 rpm, 5 min each) to remove non‐specific interactions, then resuspended in sample buffer and analyzed by Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate–Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (SDS‐PAGE). Following transfer to a nitrocellulose membrane, ubiquitinated NRF2 was detected by Western blot using an anti‐ubiquitin antibody (ab140601, Abcam, UK). A negative control was included in which an IgG antibody (#3900, Cell Signaling Technology, USA) replaced the specific NRF2 antibody.

2.19
DPN
Rat Model Construction
Eight‐week‐old male Sprague–Dawley rats (200–250 g, Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd.) were housed under standard conditions (22°C ± 1°C, 50%–60% relative humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle, free access to food and water). All animal experiments were approved by the ethics committee of our institution.
Diabetes was induced after overnight fasting by a single intravenous injection of streptozotocin (STZ, 60 mg/kg, Sigma‐Aldrich, USA) dissolved in 0.1 mol/L citrate buffer (pH 4.5). Controls received buffer alone. Seventy‐two hours later, fasting blood glucose was measured, and values > 16.7 mmol/L indicated successful induction. Rats were maintained for 8 weeks to establish DPN [
32
]. Rats were then randomly divided into four groups (
n
= 6 per group): Sham (non‐diabetic control), DPN; sh‐circ_0000756 (tail vein injection of circ_0000756 knockdown virus), and sh‐circ_0000756 + sh‐NRF2 (tail vein injection of circ_0000756 and NRF2 knockdown viruses). Body weight and glucose levels were monitored throughout the experiment [
33
].
2.20
Von Frey Filament Test
Mechanical allodynia was evaluated using an electronic Von Frey apparatus (IITC/Life Science Inc., USA). Rats were placed in acrylic chambers with a mesh floor and allowed to acclimate for 15 min. A blunt‐tip filament was applied perpendicularly to the plantar surface of the hind paws, and the minimal force eliciting paw withdrawal was recorded. Each paw was tested three times at 5‐min intervals, and the average withdrawal threshold was calculated as the paw withdrawal threshold (PWT).
2.21
Hot Plate Test
Thermal pain sensitivity was assessed using the Hargreaves apparatus (35150, Ugo Basile, Italy). Rats were placed in acrylic chambers for 15 min to acclimate before testing. A radiant heat source was applied to the plantar surface of the hind paw, and the paw withdrawal latency (PWL) was recorded. A cutoff time of 20 s was set to prevent tissue injury. Each paw was tested three times with 5‐min intervals, and the mean PWL was calculated as the thermal pain threshold.

Total RNA from sciatic nerve tissues and treated Schwann cells was extracted using TRIzol reagent (15596026, Invitrogen, USA). RNA purity was verified with a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), ensuring an A260/A280 ratio of 1.8–2.0. cDNA synthesis was performed, and RT‐qPCR was carried out with SYBR Green Master Mix (RR820A, Takara, Japan) on an ABI 7500 Real‐Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems, USA). Each 20 μL reaction contained 2 μL cDNA, 0.4 μL primers, and 10 μL SYBR Green mix. Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2
−ΔΔCt

S2

2.23
Western Blot Analysis
Total protein was extracted from Schwann cells or sciatic nerve tissues using RIPA lysis buffer (P0013B, Beyotime, China). Protein concentration was measured by bicinchoninic acid assay, and equal amounts were separated on 10% SDS‐PAGE gels and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride membranes (IPVH00010, Millipore, USA). After blocking with 5% skim milk for 1 h, membranes were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against Keap1 (1:1000, ab119403, Abcam, USA), NRF2 (1:1000, ab313825, Abcam, UK), HO‐1 (1:1000, ab68477, Abcam, UK), NQO1 (1:1000, ab80588, Abcam, UK), and β‐actin (1:5000, 20536‐1‐AP, Proteintech, USA). HRP‐conjugated secondary antibody (1:10000, SA00001‐2, Proteintech, USA) was applied for 1 h, and signals were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence using the ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (12003154, Bio‐Rad, USA).
2.24
Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) Staining
Sciatic nerve tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, dehydrated through graded ethanol, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 5 μm. Sections were deparaffinized with xylene, rehydrated, and stained with hematoxylin for 5 min, differentiated in 1% acid ethanol, blued, and counterstained with eosin for 3 min. Slides were mounted with neutral resin and examined under a Leica DMi8 microscope (Leica Microsystems, Germany).

Apoptosis in sciatic nerve tissues was assessed using a TUNEL assay kit (12156792910, Roche, Switzerland). After deparaffinization and rehydration, sections were treated with proteinase K for 30 min and incubated with TUNEL working solution at 37°C for 1 h in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI, and fluorescence was visualized with a Leica DMi8 microscope. The proportion of TUNEL‐positive cells was quantified using ImageJ software.

Supernatants from cultured Schwann cells and sciatic nerve homogenates were collected for ELISA quantification of tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF‐α, PT516), interleukin (IL)‐6 (PI328), and IL‐1β (PI303) (all from Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a Bio‐Rad microplate reader (Bio‐Rad, USA). Cytokine concentrations were determined based on a standard curve.

Oxidative Stress Biomarker Detection
Oxidative stress markers in treated cells and sciatic nerve tissues were measured using commercial kits for superoxide dismutase (SOD, A001‐3‐2), malondialdehyde (MDA, E‐BC‐K028‐M), and glutathione (GSH, E‐BC‐K097‐S) (all from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China). SOD activity was assessed by its oxygen radical scavenging ability (absorbance at 450 nm), MDA concentration by the thiobarbituric acid reaction (532 nm), and GSH by a reduction reaction (405 nm). Absorbance was measured using a Bio‐Rad microplate reader.

Introduction
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is one of the most common chronic complications of diabetes, affecting more than half of diabetic patients [
1
,
2
]. The main symptoms include sensory abnormalities, chronic pain, numbness, and nerve dysfunction, which in severe cases may progress to diabetic foot ulcers or even amputation, significantly reducing the quality of life [
3
,
4
]. Currently, the treatment of DPN primarily relies on blood glucose control and symptomatic therapy, but the irreversibility of nerve damage limits the effectiveness of treatment [
5
]. Moreover, the development of DPN is not only related to elevated blood glucose levels but also involves oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and mitochondrial dysfunction [
6
,
7
,
8
]. Since the exact pathogenesis of DPN is not yet fully understood, identifying new molecular targets to improve nerve damage holds significant clinical importance. In recent years, the regulatory roles of non‐coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in diabetes and its complications have attracted increasing attention. Among them, circular RNAs (circRNAs), due to their stability and widespread expression, may play a key role in the pathology of DPN [
9
]. This study aims to screen specific circRNAs based on a DPN animal model and explore their potential regulatory mechanisms, providing new insights for the intervention of DPN.
The pathological development of DPN involves complex molecular mechanisms, with oxidative stress recognized as a central pathogenic factor [
10
]. Exposure to high glucose (HG) conditions promotes the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which disrupt neuronal cell membranes and impair mitochondrial function, ultimately inducing neuronal apoptosis [
11
,
12
]. In addition, inflammatory responses and neurovascular dysfunction further contribute to disease progression [
13
,
14
]. Recent studies have found that DPN‐related nerve damage persists even after normalization of blood glucose levels, a phenomenon termed metabolic memory. This persistence may be driven by epigenetic modifications, sustained activation of inflammatory mediators, and regulatory effects of non‐coding RNAs [
15
,
16
,
17
]. Schwann cells, as key supportive cells in the peripheral nervous system, play an important role in the initiation and progression of DPN. The metabolic dysregulation of these cells under HG conditions has been proposed as a key factor underlying the long‐term persistence of DPN [
18
,
19
]. Investigation of the metabolic regulatory mechanisms in Schwann cells, particularly the molecular determinants of metabolic memory, is essential for elucidating the chronic course of DPN.
circRNAs represent a distinct class of ncRNAs, characterized by a covalently closed circular structure that provides high stability and enables important regulatory functions in diverse diseases [
20
]. Accumulating evidence indicates that circRNAs exert their effects through the competitive endogenous RNA (ceRNA) mechanism, binding to miRNAs and influencing the expression of target genes, thereby influencing oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic homeostasis [
21
,
22
,
23
]. CircRNAs have emerged as promising regulatory factors in metabolic diseases, as their dysregulated expression is directly associated with disease progression. For example, in obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, circRNAs influence glucose and lipid homeostasis, insulin resistance, and inflammatory processes [
21
,
24
]. Their structural stability and evolutionary conservation further support their potential as reliable biomarkers and therapeutic targets [
25
]. Several circRNAs have been implicated in diabetic complications. For example, the roles of circHIPK3 and circANKRD36 in diabetic nephropathy have been reported [
9
,
26
]. However, research on circRNAs in DPN remains limited.
In this study, RNA sequencing was performed to analyze the circRNA expression profile of sciatic nerve tissues from DPN rats, and the sequencing data were further subjected to systematic analysis using Weighted Gene Co‐expression Network Analysis (WGCNA). This method identifies co‐expression modules based on similarities in expression patterns across large‐scale transcriptomic data and screens for hub circRNAs occupying key regulatory positions, thereby unbiasedly revealing potential molecular regulatory networks closely associated with disease pathogenesis [
27
]. Among these, circ_0000756 was identified and its critical role in DPN was investigated. Preliminary analyses suggest that circ_0000756 may influence miR‐7b through a ceRNA mechanism, thereby modulating the NRF2/ARE signaling pathway and promoting oxidative stress and neuronal injury.
Therefore, this study was designed to systematically elucidate the role of circ_0000756 in DPN and to uncover its underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms. Specifically, we focused on whether circ_0000756 modulates the NRF2/ARE axis through a ceRNA mechanism and thereby influences metabolic memory. To this end, we employed both in vitro and in vivo approaches, including an HG Schwann cell model, circRNA knockdown or overexpression assays, and a DPN rat model, to evaluate the impact of circ_0000756 on neuronal injury. Through these experiments, we further sought to verify whether circ_0000756 exerts its effects by sponging miR‐7b, suppressing NRF2/ARE signaling, and thereby regulating oxidative stress and metabolic memory in DPN. Collectively, the findings from this study are expected to clarify the pivotal role of circRNAs in the pathogenesis of DPN and to provide novel insights into early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention. Notably, circ_0000756 may represent a promising therapeutic target, offering theoretical support for the development of precision medicine in diabetic neurological complications.

Discussion
This study systematically elucidated the mechanism of circ_0000756 in DPN through a multi‐omics approach, incorporating RNA‐Seq, WGCNA, proteomics, and metabolomics. The findings demonstrated that circ_0000756 was significantly upregulated in the sciatic nerve of DPN model rats and exerted its effects through a ceRNA mechanism by suppressing miR‐7b, thereby inhibiting the NRF2/ARE signaling pathway. This suppression resulted in elevated oxidative stress, exacerbated Schwann cell damage, and intensified neuroinflammatory responses. Moreover, metabolomics analysis revealed that high glucose exposure induced persistent metabolic alterations in Schwann cells even after glucose normalization, highlighting a metabolic memory effect. Notably, circ_0000756 downregulation mitigated this effect, suggesting its critical role in sustaining metabolic dysregulation. Functional experiments demonstrated that circ_0000756 regulates Schwann cell viability, apoptosis, and oxidative stress in vitro, while in vivo studies confirmed its contribution to nerve injury in DPN rats. Collectively, these findings identify circ_0000756 as a critical driver of DPN pathogenesis and provide mechanistic insights into how it regulates metabolic memory via the NRF2/ARE axis, offering a novel perspective for understanding and potentially treating DPN.
In recent years, circRNAs have emerged as critical regulatory factors in various diseases due to their stable circular structure and extensive regulatory functions [
39
,
40
]. Studies have shown that circHIPK3 and circANKRD36 play essential roles in diabetic nephropathy and diabetic retinopathy, primarily by modulating miRNA activity through the ceRNA mechanism, thereby influencing glucose metabolism, oxidative stress, and inflammation [
26
,
41
,
42
]. However, the specific functions of circRNAs in DPN remain largely unexplored. Previous studies have primarily focused on miRNA regulation in DPN, demonstrating that miR‐146a and miR‐124 can modulate inflammatory responses and neuroprotection [
43
,
44
]. However, how circRNAs regulate these miRNAs and their downstream pathways remains unclear. In this study, WGCNA was used to identify DPN‐associated circRNAs co‐expression modules, leading to the first identification of circ_0000756 and its functional characterization in DPN. In contrast to previous studies that mainly focused on mitochondrial damage or neurovascular dysfunction, circHIPK3 has been reported to be predominantly expressed in serum and the central nervous system, where it regulates neuroinflammation and pain pathways through miR‐124 [
45
]. In addition, circ_0002538 functions as a sponge for miR‐138‐5p to regulate plasmolipin expression, which in vitro promotes Schwann cell migration and myelination, thereby alleviating DPN symptoms [
46
]. This study highlights the role of circRNAs in regulating Schwann cell metabolic homeostasis and oxidative stress, thereby broadening our understanding of DPN pathogenesis. In addition, no expression signals of circHIPK3 or circANKRD36 were detected in the sciatic nerve circRNA sequencing data of DPN rats in this study. This finding suggests that, unlike circRNAs previously reported in other diabetic complications such as diabetic nephropathy, circ_0000756 may exhibit DPN‐specific expression characteristics, further underscoring its significance as a potential novel biomarker and regulatory molecule.
Oxidative stress is a key factor in the pathological progression of DPN. Previous studies have demonstrated that the NRF2/ARE signaling pathway serves as a central defense mechanism against oxidative stress, with NRF2 activation inducing the expression of antioxidant genes such as HO‐1, NQO1, and GCLC, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and inflammation [
47
,
48
,
49
]. Several studies have reported that NRF2 activity is impaired in DPN, leading to reduced antioxidant capacity and exacerbated neuronal damage [
13
,
50
]. The present study identified circ_0000756 as a novel regulator of NRF2, functioning through a ceRNA mechanism to inhibit miR‐7b, which subsequently suppresses NRF2 expression and weakens the antioxidant response. In contrast to previous research that primarily emphasized the role of NRF2 in DPN, the findings reveal a novel circRNA‐mediated mechanism regulating NRF2/ARE signaling via the ceRNA network. Future investigations should focus on targeting circ_0000756 or miR‐7b to enhance NRF2 signaling, thereby offering promising therapeutic avenues for DPN intervention.
The metabolic memory effect refers to the persistent cellular damage and functional abnormalities in diabetic patients, even after blood glucose levels are controlled. This phenomenon has been extensively reported in diabetic nephropathy and cardiovascular complications [
17
,
51
]. In contrast, research on metabolic memory in DPN remains limited [
15
,
52
]. Metabolomics analysis in the present study demonstrated that Schwann cells retain metabolic alterations following high‐glucose exposure, even after restoration of normoglycemia, suggesting that metabolic memory may contribute to the chronic progression of DPN. Further investigations revealed that circ_0000756 upregulation sustains these metabolic abnormalities, whereas its knockdown partially reverses metabolic dysregulation. Circ_0000756 functions as a sponge for miR‐7b, resulting in Keap1 upregulation and NRF2 downregulation, thereby maintaining oxidative stress despite glucose normalization. This persistent redox imbalance reinforces the phenomenon of metabolic memory in DPN. The present study provides the first evidence implicating circRNAs in maintaining metabolic memory in DPN, offering new insights into long‐term intervention strategies and highlighting circRNAs as promising therapeutic targets.
The ceRNA network has emerged as a significant research focus in molecular biology [
53
]. Numerous studies have confirmed that circRNAs can function as miRNA sponges, indirectly regulating mRNA expression levels. However, research on ceRNA networks in DPN remains in its early stages [
54
,
55
]. Through bioinformatics analysis and molecular experiments, this study identified the circ_0000756‐miR‐7b‐NRF2/ARE axis as a key regulatory pathway in DPN, consistent with previous findings highlighting the neuroprotective role of miR‐7b [
56
]. Unlike previous studies that focused on miRNA‐mediated regulation of transcription factors [
57
], this study further elucidates the upstream regulatory role of circRNAs in DPN.
This study revealed that in metabolic memory‐associated DPN, circ_0000756 acts as a miR‐7b sponge, leading to Keap1 upregulation, enhanced NRF2 ubiquitination and degradation, and subsequent suppression of NRF2/ARE pathway activation. This mechanism was validated in both Schwann cell oxidative stress models and DPN animal models. Circ_0000756 silencing significantly reduced Keap1 expression and enhanced NRF2/ARE pathway activity, thereby alleviating oxidative stress, inhibiting apoptosis and inflammatory responses, and improving DPN pathophysiology. These findings highlight circ_0000756 as a critical upstream regulator of the NRF2/ARE signaling pathway, demonstrating its potential role in neuroprotection. This study offers a new therapeutic target for DPN, advancing both mechanistic research and clinical intervention strategies.
This study is the first to identify the critical role of the circ_0000756‐miR‐7b‐Keap1‐NRF2 axis in DPN, enriching the molecular pathophysiological framework of DPN. Silencing circ_0000756 alleviates oxidative stress‐induced damage by activating the NRF2/ARE signaling pathway, providing a scientific basis for the development of novel RNA interference therapies. This mechanism holds potential clinical value, offering a new therapeutic strategy to improve neurological function and quality of life in DPN patients, while also providing insights applicable to other oxidative stress‐related neurodegenerative disorders.
The current findings are primarily derived from cellular and animal models, and clinical validation remains absent. Moreover, whether circ_0000756 exerts tissue‐specific functions or regulates additional signaling pathways has not yet been clarified. Future research should prioritize clinical translation, including the design of circ_0000756‐targeted therapeutic agents and systematic evaluation of their safety and efficacy in human patients. A comprehensive exploration of circRNA regulatory networks will be crucial for refining the mechanistic understanding of DPN and expanding therapeutic options.
